title: Commonitorium De Coelestio Imperatori Oblatum
author: Marius Mercator
source: Translated by Claude from tmp772.tmp772.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: 1. Ut autem et Pelagius cum ipso [Bal. isto] pari- ter damnaretur, istud in causa est. Ausus est memo- ratus ante a vastationem urbis Romae in apostolum Paulum b commentarios condere, c et his edere, de quorum amicitia praesumebat;
passages.english: 1. Now the reason why Pelagius too was condemned together with him is this. Before the sack of the city of Rome, the man mentioned dared to compose commentaries on the apostle Paul, and to publish them to those on whose friendship he relied;
passages.notes: "[Bal. isto]" is an editorial variant note (Baluze reads "isto" for "ipso") and is not translated. The stray letters a, b, c are footnote marks and have been omitted. "his edere" is taken as "to publish [them] to these people" (i.e. to his friends).

passages.original: Illud quoque, quod superius positum est capi- tulum, sentiri, a Coelestio, et esse consentaneum magistri sui doctrinae memoravimus, id est, « Legem sic mittere ad regnum coelorum, sicut Evangelium; » Pelagius quibusdam scriptis suis aperte confirmat atque pronuntiat.
passages.english: That too which was set down above as a heading, and which we have stated is held by Caelestius and is consistent with his master's teaching, namely, "that the Law sends [one] to the kingdom of heaven just as the Gospel does," Pelagius openly confirms and declares in certain of his writings.
passages.notes: Coelestius is the heretic Caelestius, a follower of Pelagius.

passages.original: 5. Manifestum est enim, secundum Pelagium, quia si sub eodem vel simili adhuc sumus vinculo, etiam sub Evangelii tempore; a et si quid tamquam homines erraverimus, aut unum de praeceptis Evan- gelii non impleverimus,b esse nos maledictos. Quod si ita, quod absit, tamen ut ille vult sit dictum, ex- aequatum est legi veteri Evangelium; et ubi erit di- ctum Pauli Apostoli : Christus nos redemit de male- dicto legis factus pro nobis maledictum, quia scriptum est ( Deut, xxvii, 26 ) : Maledictus omnis homo, qui non permanet in omnibus quae scripta sunt in libro legit, ut faciat ea (Galat, iii, 10).
passages.english: 5. For it is clear, according to Pelagius, that if we are still under the same or a similar bond even in the time of the Gospel, then if we have erred in anything, as human beings do, or have not fulfilled one of the precepts of the Gospel, we are accursed. But if this were so (God forbid!), and were said as he wishes, the Gospel has been made equal to the old Law; and where then will be the saying of the apostle Paul: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us, because it is written (Deut. 27:26): Cursed is every man who does not abide by all the things that are written in the book of the Law, to do them" (Gal. 3:10)?
passages.notes: Footnote marks a, b omitted. "legit" is a scanning error for "legis". The citation joins Gal. 3:13 and Gal. 3:10, though the edition gives only Gal. 3:10.

passages.original: De tempore aliquid hinc opinor colligi probabiliter posse. Scripsit Mercator post Theodori Mopsuesteni mortem, ut constat ex his verbis (Initio Prologi seu Commonitorii) : A Theodoro quondam episcopo oppidi Mopsue- steni; immo post obitum S. Augustini: Sanctae recordationis Augustinus episcopus diversis temporibus, etc.; atque etiam post vulgatam ipsius responsionem ad opus postremum Juliani. Sic enim Mercator (Ibid., sub fi- nem) : Sanctus Augustinus sex suis libris quatuor priores illius evertit, octo quoque posteriores singulis re- sponsionibus suis ad singula capita subjectis : quod utriusque Opus cum In manus nostras venisset, etc.
passages.english: From this, I think, something can with probability be gathered about the date. Mercator wrote after the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia, as is clear from these words (at the beginning of the Prologue or Commonitorium): "By Theodore, formerly bishop of the town of Mopsuestia"; indeed, after the death of St. Augustine: "Augustine, bishop of holy memory, at various times," etc.; and also after the publication of his reply to Julian's last work. For Mercator says this (ibid., near the end): "St. Augustine overturned the first four books of that man in six books of his own, and the latter eight as well, with his replies set beneath each chapter one by one: and when the work of each of them had come into our hands," etc.
passages.notes: Scanning hyphenations (Mopsue- steni, fi- nem, re- sponsionibus) read as whole words; "In manus" read as "in manus". "Quondam" may mean "the late" rather than "formerly".
